title: She Said “It Is Well” While Her World Was Falling Apart
paragraphs:
She Said “It Is Well” While Her World Was Falling Apart
Why the Shunammite Woman Refused to Panic—and What She Knew About God That Most People Still Don't
There are moments in life when panic feels more natural than faith.
Moments when the doctor goes silent.
When the phone rings too late.
When the marriage begins cracking.
When the child you prayed for starts drifting.
When the future you imagined collapses in a single afternoon.
Most people know how to trust God when everything is going well.
The real question is what happens when everything suddenly isn't.
That is why the story of the Shunammite woman continues to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because this is not merely a story about a miracle.
It is a story about a woman who stared directly into devastation and somehow refused to surrender her confidence in God.
Her story is found in 2 Kings 4, and the details are astonishing.
She was a wealthy woman from Shunem who showed extraordinary hospitality to the prophet Elisha. Seeing him regularly pass through her region, she and her husband prepared a room specifically for him.
No publicity.
No recognition.
No platform.
Just faithfulness.
God noticed.
Through Elisha, God promised her something she had likely stopped hoping for long ago.
A son.
The promise came true.
Year after year she watched the child grow.
The gift of God became part of her daily life.
Then one ordinary day everything changed.
The boy complained of a pain in his head while working with his father.
Hours later he died in his mother's arms.
Imagine that moment.
The room grows quiet.
The body becomes still.
The promise appears broken.
The future disappears.
The dream God gave seems buried before your eyes.
Yet what happened next is one of the most remarkable demonstrations of faith found anywhere in Scripture.
The Hebrew text records that when others asked how she was doing, she answered:
"שָׁלוֹם" (Shalom)
Often translated as "It is well."
The Hebrew concept of shalom is much deeper than simple peace.
It means completeness.
Wholeness.
Harmony.
A state where God remains sovereign even when circumstances seem chaotic.
This was not denial.
This was not pretending everything was okay.
Her son was dead.
The crisis was real.
The pain was real.
The tears were real.
But her faith was also real.
Many people think faith means never feeling afraid.
Biblically, faith means refusing to let fear become your master.
The Shunammite woman never claimed to understand what God was doing.
She simply refused to conclude that God had stopped working.
Notice something extraordinary.
She did not immediately prepare a funeral.
She did not surrender to despair.
She did not spend her energy rehearsing worst-case scenarios.
She went directly to the man of God.
Directly toward the source of God's promise.
Directly toward hope.
There is a lesson here that many of us desperately need.
When life falls apart, people often run everywhere except toward God.
We run toward anxiety.
Toward endless scrolling.
Toward distractions.
Toward addictions.
Toward bitterness.
Toward self-reliance.
Toward panic.
The Shunammite woman ran toward God.
That decision changed everything.
Eventually she arrived before Elisha and poured out her grief.
This is another beautiful truth hidden in the story.
Faith is not emotional suppression.
God never asks us to pretend.
The woman who said "It is well" also wept.
She also grieved.
She also spoke honestly about her pain.
Biblical faith does not require fake smiles.
It requires genuine trust.
Many believers today are exhausted because they think faith means acting as if nothing hurts.
That is not what Scripture teaches.
King David cried.
Jeremiah cried.
Job cried.
Even Jesus cried.
At the tomb of Lazarus, Scripture records the shortest verse in the Bible:
"Jesus wept." (John 11:35)
In Greek, "ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς" (Edakrysen ho Iēsous).
The Son of God stood fully aware that resurrection was minutes away, yet He still entered human sorrow.
That changes everything.
Your tears do not disqualify your faith.
Sometimes your tears are evidence of it.
When Elisha eventually arrived and prayed, God restored the child's life.
The promise that seemed dead was alive again.
The impossible became possible.
The story reminds us of a pattern that appears throughout the Bible.
God specializes in resurrection.
Abraham and Sarah's hope looked dead.
God revived it.
Joseph's future looked dead.
God revived it.
Israel's nation looked dead.
God revived it.
Lazarus looked dead.
Jesus revived him.
The cross appeared to be the death of God's plan.
Then came the resurrection.
This is why the Gospel is not merely good advice.
It is good news.
At the center of Christianity stands a Savior who repeatedly demonstrates that apparent endings are not always actual endings.
The New Testament word for grace is the Greek word "χάρις" (charis).
Grace is God's unearned favor.
His undeserved kindness.
His willingness to rewrite stories people thought were finished.
No one embodies that truth more fully than Jesus Christ.
The woman from Shunem experienced restoration.
But every restoration in Scripture ultimately points forward to Christ.
Because the greatest resurrection was never her son's resurrection.
The greatest resurrection was Jesus walking out of the tomb.
The greatest miracle was not merely a child receiving life again.
The greatest miracle is sinners receiving eternal life through Him.
Perhaps that is why this ancient story still feels so personal.
Maybe your dream feels dead.
Maybe your marriage feels dead.
Maybe your faith feels weak.
Maybe your future feels uncertain.
Maybe you are carrying a burden nobody else sees.
The Shunammite woman's story does not guarantee that every earthly outcome will unfold exactly the way we hope.
But it does reveal something unchanging about God.
He remains trustworthy when circumstances are not.
He remains faithful when answers are delayed.
He remains present when emotions are overwhelming.
He remains God when everything else feels unstable.
The Hebrew name often used throughout the Old Testament is יהוה (YHWH), commonly rendered as Yahweh.
The covenant-keeping God.
The God who does not abandon His people.
The God who keeps writing when everyone else thinks the story is over.
That truth reaches its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is the ultimate "It is well."
Not because life is always easy.
Not because suffering is imaginary.
Not because Christians never struggle.
But because Christ has overcome sin, death, hell, and the grave.
Through Him, even our deepest wounds can become testimonies.
Even our failures can become ministries.
Even our scandals can become stories of grace.
If this message touched something deep inside your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
You never know who is silently carrying a burden that feels impossible to bear.
What area of your life are you trusting God with right now?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Your support helps advance this ministry and allows us to continue producing resources that point people to Christ.
The miracle wasn't that she never felt fear.
The miracle was that fear never became her god.
